title: Benji and Dot's Rough & Smooth Box
markdown:
Benji was the most careful gardener you ever did see. He would stop to admire a tiny sprout growing sideways and then gently coax it to grow straight up. He always wore his bright green hat, and it was always, always perfectly straight.

Dot the ladybird was a little explorer with a back as red as a strawberry and perfectly round black spots. She’d zoom and zip and flit about, looking for the juiciest dewdrops and the most delightful dandelions.

Mr. Hale was the kindest gentleman, with a waistcoat that twinkled like a sky full of tiny happy stars. When he smiled, it was as warm as sunshine on a summer afternoon.

It was Mr. Hale’s birthday. Benji wanted to make him the most spectacular, the most stupendous, the most treasure-y treasure box that had ever been. He had found a lovely wooden box, just waiting to be covered in wonderful things.

But oh dear. Benji only had a jumble of bits and bobs he’d collected. Little pebbles as bumpy as a grumpy troll’s knees. Fluffy moss like a tiny green squishy cloud. Shells so smooth and shiny they felt like cool slippery soap. Pieces of bark as rough and scratchy as a giant cat’s tongue.

Benji let out a big gardener’s sigh, which sounded a little like wind rustling through dry leaves. “Oh, fiddlesticks,” he mumbled, looking at his collection.

He tried to stick a shiny shell onto the smooth lid of the box. Slip! It slid right off. He tried to press a fuzzy bit of moss onto a bumpy pebble. Plop! It wouldn’t stick at all.

“These bits just don’t want to play together,” he grumbled. “They don’t make a nice pattern at all. The bumpy ones and the smooth ones just look… all higgledy-piggledy.”

He tried sticking a scratchy piece of bark right next to a shiny shell. It looked all wrong, like trying to wear one slipper on your head. He wanted it to look neat and pretty, like a perfectly planted row of flowers.

Just then, a little whizz-pop sound, and Dot the ladybird landed right on the tip of Benji’s nose.

“What’s all this sighing and moping about, Benji?” she chirped, her voice as bright as a little tinkling bell. She was always up for a bit of an adventure, and Benji looking glum was an invitation.

“It’s this treasure box, Dot,” Benji explained, pointing with a finger peeking out of his gardening glove. “I want it to be super-duper special for Mr. Hale, but all these decorating bits are just too… different. They don’t stick together nicely, and they don’t make a pretty picture when I try to put them on.”

Benji, being Benji, could probably spend an hour just admiring how one pebble was exactly the same shade of grey as a grumpy cloud.

Dot wiggled her little antennae, which always meant she was thinking very hard. She scurried down Benji’s arm, and then, tip-tap-tip-tap-tip-tap, she went exploring across the pile of treasures.

First she walked over a crunchy pebble. “Ooh!” she exclaimed. “That feels so bumpy and tingly under my little feet! It feels like it has a thousand tiny hills and valleys!”

Then, scootle-scootle-scootle, she went onto a shiny shell. “Whoa! This is so slippy-slidey and smooth! Wheee!” she giggled, doing a little shimmy.

She tiptoed onto the fluffy moss. “Mmm, so soft and gentle, like a tiny cozy bed!”

And finally, scritch-scratch-scritch, she went on the rough bark. “My, oh my! That’s quite rough and prickly, like a little hedgehog!”

She crawled back up to Benji’s chin, doing a little happy dance. “Benji!” she buzzed, her little legs tickling him. “You know what? These bits aren’t just different. They feel really, really different. Super different!”

Benji blinked his big careful eyes. “Different how, Dot?”

“Well,” said Dot, puffing out her little chest. “Some bits feel like they have a hundred tiny prickles all over them. They’re all bumpy and uneven and catch on things. We call that rough!”

Benji’s eyebrows wiggled under his perfectly straight green hat. Rough? That was a new word.

“And,” Dot continued, even more excited, “other bits feel like a quiet still pond. They’re so flat and nice and easy to slide on. They’re smooth!”

Smooth! Benji’s face lit up like a tiny sunflower bursting into bloom. He looked at the pile of treasures again. He picked up a piece of bark. “This is rough!” he declared, feeling it carefully with his gloved finger. Then he picked up a shell. “And this is smooth!”

He looked at his hands, then at the wooden box, and then he had the most brilliant idea. It popped into his head just like a bubble.

“Dot, you amazing ladybird, you’re a genius!” Benji exclaimed, happy but still careful not to startle anyone.

He started to arrange the bits with purpose. He put all the rough scratchy bark pieces along one side of the box. It made a strong interesting edge, like the sturdy trunk of a tree, and the roughness gave the glue something to really hold onto. Then he took the smooth shiny shells and placed them on top, where they glittered and gleamed like tiny fallen stars against the rough bark. Because the bark was rough, the glue could catch; because the shells were smooth, they shone. Next he carefully arranged the soft fluffy moss in between the bark and shells, looking like little green pillows for sleepy bugs. The moss stuck well to the rough bark.

He even used the crunchy pebbles to make a wiggly border. He noticed something really cool. The bumpy pebbles fit nicely into the slightly rougher surface of the bark, like puzzle pieces. And the smooth shells looked even more shiny and sparkly next to the soft quiet moss.

It wasn’t higgledy-piggledy anymore. It looked absolutely beautiful. The rough bits made the smooth bits look even smoother and more special, and the smooth bits made the rough bits look wonderfully interesting.

“Hooray! Hooray!” cheered Dot, flying in little happy circles around Benji’s head. “It looks amazing, Benji! The bestest box ever!”

Benji beamed, his green hat almost tipping over with pure joy. “You’re right, Dot! By noticing how different things feel — rough and smooth — we can make something really, truly special.”

When Mr. Hale opened the treasure box, his eyes sparkled even brighter than his waistcoat. “Oh, Benji!” he boomed, his voice like warm sweet honey. “This is the most wonderful treasure box I have ever, ever seen! I love how you’ve made the rough bits and the smooth bits fit together so perfectly. It feels so interesting to touch!”

Benji and Dot smiled at each other, a perfect team. Benji ran one careful finger along bark, then shell, then moss. Rough. Smooth. Soft. The birthday box sat on Mr. Hale’s table, and the green hat, for once, sat just a tiny bit crooked, which was exactly right.
